title: And That’s How I Found Mine
excerpt: When you're in love you always wish that something good will happen…
body:
When you're in love you always wish that something good will happen — a message, a glance, a reason to believe the ordinary day might turn luminous.

I used to look for love in grand gestures. Later I learned it lives in quieter places: the shared silence, the remembered coffee order, the way someone says your name when the room is full.

And that’s how I found mine — not all at once, but in pieces that somehow knew how to fit.

title: That Time Of The Month
excerpt: I struggle to even eat, To walk, to run, to survive…
body:
I struggle to even eat,
To walk, to run, to survive —
And still the world asks me
to smile like nothing is happening inside.

That time of the month
is not a punchline.
It is a body negotiating with itself,
a quiet weather system
no one else can feel.

Be gentle.
With her.
With yourself.

title: To The One I Loved
excerpt: To The One I Loved, How have you been? … I kind of miss you…
body:
To The One I Loved,

How have you been?
I hope the days are kinder to you than they sometimes were to us.

I kind of miss you — not in the way that asks you to return, but in the way a favourite song returns without warning.

If you ever wonder whether you mattered: you did.
You still do, in the soft archive of who I became after you.

Take care.
Always.

title: Still I Rise
excerpt: After every falling, a quieter standing — still, I rise.
body:
They said the night would keep me.
It almost did.

But morning has a stubborn habit
of arriving anyway —
and so do I.

After every falling,
a quieter standing.
Still,
I rise.

title: Forever We Said
excerpt: Forever was easy to say when the streetlights were still on.
body:
Forever we said —
as if the word were a bridge
and not a weather report.

Forever was easy
when the streetlights were still on
and neither of us had learned
how silence can arrive
wearing love’s old coat.

I keep the word anyway.
Not as a promise.
As a scar that learned to glow.

title: It Hurts To Love You
excerpt: It hurts to love you — and somehow that is still not a reason to stop.
body:
It hurts to love you
the way winter hurts a window —
clear, inevitable,
beautifully inconvenient.

I keep choosing the view.
I keep choosing you.
Even when choosing
means aching.

title: जिंदगी एक ही मिली है।
excerpt: जिंदगी एक ही मिली है — इसे अधूरा मत छोड़ना।
body:
जिंदगी एक ही मिली है।
इसे डर के खाते में मत जमा करना।

कुछ बातें अधूरी रह जाएँगी —
यह भी सच है।
पर जो कहा जा सकता है,
आज कह देना।

एक ही जिंदगी है।
इसे महसूस करना।

title: Shree Krishna Quotes from Bhagavad Gita
excerpt: Lines from the Gita that steady the mind when the day feels uneven.
body:
“You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work.”

“The mind is restless and difficult to restrain, but it is subdued by practice.”

“Whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, I manifest myself.”

Keep what steadies you. Leave the rest on the page.

title: This Is Why I Hate To Fall In Love Again
excerpt: Because loving again means handing someone the map to every soft place.
body:
This is why I hate to fall in love again:
because the heart has a terrible memory for maps.

It remembers every soft place.
It forgets every warning.

And still —
some evenings smell like possibility,
and I walk toward the old mistake
as if it were a new country.

title: 7 Things Every Single Person Will Relate To During Valentine’s Week
excerpt: From muted stories to ordered desserts for one — the soft comedy of being single in February.
body:
1. Suddenly everyone is a poet.
2. Your phone becomes a museum of couple posts.
3. You consider adopting a plant and naming it after a feeling.
4. Chocolate tastes like solidarity.
5. You rewrite your bio, then undo it.
6. You text your friends more than usual — and mean it.
7. You remember: being alone is not the same as being unfinished.

Happy your week — however you spend it.

title: A Story For Rainy Evenings
excerpt: She kept the window open so the rain could finish the sentence she couldn’t.
body:
She kept the window open so the rain could finish the sentence she couldn’t.

On the table: half a letter, a cold cup, and the kind of silence that is not empty — only waiting.

When the power flickered, she laughed once, quietly, as if the city had finally agreed to sit with her.

By morning the letter was still unfinished.
But something in her had moved an inch toward kindness.
Sometimes that is the whole story.

title: Lines We Keep
excerpt: Not every sentence needs an audience. Some only need a notebook.
body:
Not every sentence needs an audience.
Some only need a notebook.

Keep the line that makes your shoulders drop.
Keep the one that tells the truth without raising its voice.

The rest can wait.

title: Notes From A Kolkata Rain
excerpt: The tram wires shine like sentences waiting for a reader.
body:
The tram wires shine
like sentences waiting for a reader.

Rain writes on the tram window
in a language I almost know.

Somewhere between Howrah and home
I become a quieter version of myself —
the kind who listens
before answering the sky.

title: The Case For Softness
excerpt: Arguments win rooms. Softness wins the people you still want tomorrow.
body:
I was trained to make airtight arguments.
Life kept handing me people who needed air.

Softness is not the absence of a spine.
It is knowing when to set the brief down
and ask how their day really went.

Some verdicts matter less
than the hand you hold after.

title: Stories We Don’t Tell At Dinner
excerpt: Behind every polite smile is a paragraph that never got a turn to speak.
body:
Behind every polite smile is a paragraph that never got a turn to speak.

She passed the salt, laughed at the right jokes, and kept the unheard story folded in her napkin — the one about almost leaving, almost saying, almost becoming someone braver.

Later, alone, she wrote it down.
That is how unheard stories survive:
not at the table,
but on the page.

title: Since I Was Nine
excerpt: I started writing before I knew what publishing meant — only that the page listened.
body:
I started writing before I knew what publishing meant — only that the page listened.

Ranchi evenings, a cheap notebook, and the stubborn belief that a sentence could rearrange a day.

Years later the notebooks stack higher,
but the reason is the same:
to make the unsaid bearable
by giving it a shape.

title: Quiet Thoughts, Loud Evenings
excerpt: My thoughts arrive like handwriting — uneven, honest, mine.
body:
My thoughts arrive like handwriting —
uneven, honest, mine.

Ahmedabad heat outside;
inside, a cooler kind of weather
where feelings get named
before they harden into silence.

I write them down
so they don’t have to shout.

title: Between Neral And Mumbai
excerpt: The commute is a long corridor of almosts — almost home, almost grown, almost said.
body:
The commute is a long corridor of almosts —
almost home, almost grown, almost said.

Windows blur towns into one continuous maybe.
I write in the margins of the journey
because the destination keeps changing names.

Between Neral and Mumbai
I learn that becoming
is also a kind of arriving.

title: Stand For The Page
excerpt: To every writer who almost deleted the draft — keep the line that scared you.
body:
To every writer who almost deleted the draft —

Keep the line that scared you.
Keep the one that told the truth without apology.

The page does not need perfection.
It needs your standing.

From Rishikesh to wherever you are reading this:
your words are allowed to take up space.

title: A Family Of Voices
excerpt: We are not competing for the same sentence — we are building a chorus.
body:
We are not competing for the same sentence —
we are building a chorus.

Some of us write soft.
Some of us write sharp.
All of us write because something refused to stay unsaid.

Welcome to the family of voices.

title: What We Leave Unsaid
excerpt: Dear reader — the silence between us is full of almost-sentences.
body:
Dear reader,

The silence between us is full of almost-sentences.
I am learning to finish a few of them here.

If this reaches you on a day when words feel heavy,
set the phone down, breathe, and remember:
not every feeling needs an audience —
but every feeling deserves a place.

Yours,
in the unfinished phrase.
